hooks: California was a fictional island in a 1510 Spanish romance, ruled by a queen called Calafia — explorers applied the name here believing the peninsula was an island.
Tijuana in it is one of the busiest border crossings in the world.
Its Valle de Guadalupe produces about 70% of Mexican wine, in a Mediterranean pocket 100 km from the desert.
Uncertain: possibly from a mispronounced Opata word, or from Spanish señora after a shrine image.
The largest desert state, and the Sonoran desert in it is the only place the saguaro cactus grows.
It borders Arizona, raises much of Mexico's beef, and the Seri people on its coast speak a language related to no other.
Probably Nahuatl or Tarahumara for "dry sandy place" or "between two waters"; the dog is named after the state, not the other way round.
The largest state in Mexico, bigger than the United Kingdom.
Copper Canyon in it is deeper and larger than the Grand Canyon, and the railway through it climbs 2,400 m with 86 tunnels.
From a Nahuatl word, possibly "place of many trees" or a local people's name; its full title adds "de Zaragoza" for the general who won at Puebla.
It has the longest stretch of the US border of any Mexican state.
Its Cuatro Ciénegas basin holds pools with species found nowhere else, studied as an analogue for early life on Earth.
"New León", named in 1582 after the kingdom of León in Spain.
Monterrey in it is Mexico's industrial capital and has the highest income per head of any large Mexican city.
The Cerro de la Silla, a saddle-shaped mountain, stands over Monterrey and is the city's emblem.
The southern half of the same Californian peninsula, split off as a state in 1974.
The whole Gulf of California along it is a UNESCO site; Cousteau called it the world's aquarium.
Grey whales come to its lagoons at San Ignacio and Ojo de Liebre to calve, after swimming down from the Arctic.
From Huastec tamaholipa, roughly "place where people pray" — tam- is a Huastec place prefix.
Its Sierra de Tamaulipas and El Cielo reserve are where tropical, desert and temperate zones meet, which makes for unusual bird lists.
It has the second-longest US border, and the Rio Grande forms all of it.
From a Cahita phrase, roughly "round pitahaya cactus" — sina, a pitahaya, and lobola, round.
It is Mexico's vegetable garden: most of the tomatoes the United States eats in winter come from this coast.
Banda music, brass bands playing at volume, is from here, and so is Mazatlán's carnival, the third largest in the world.
Named by a Basque founder in 1563 after Durango in the Basque Country, whose own name means "beyond the water".
Its dry canyons stood in for the American West in dozens of films, and John Wayne shot many of his here.
The Sierra Madre Occidental crossing it holds the Espinazo del Diablo, a road along a knife-edge ridge.
From Nahuatl zacatl, grass, plus -tecatl, people of — the people of the grasslands.
Silver was found here in 1546, and for two centuries this one district was among the largest silver producers in the world.
Its pink stone colonial centre is a UNESCO site, and a cable car crosses the town to the hill above it.
St Louis plus Potosí — the Bolivian silver mountain, borrowed as a boast that this one would be as rich.
Real de Catorce here is a semi-abandoned silver town reached through a 2.3 km tunnel.
Huasteca Potosina, its eastern half, is waterfalls and turquoise rivers, and the Wixárika make a 400 km pilgrimage across the state each year.
"Hot waters", for the thermal springs the city was founded on in 1575.
The smallest mainland state, and much of its old city is undermined by tunnels nobody has fully mapped.
Its San Marcos fair is the oldest and largest in Mexico, running since 1828.
Named for Nayar, a Cora chief and later a god — the Cora resisted Spanish rule here until 1722.
The Wixárika (Huichol) live in its sierra and are known for yarn paintings and beadwork made with peyote visions.
Its Marietas islands have a beach at the bottom of a crater, opened by military bomb testing a century ago.
From Purépecha kuanasï-uato, "place of frogs", for rock formations that look like them.
Its silver mine, La Valenciana, produced perhaps two thirds of the world's silver in its best years.
Mexico's independence war began in Dolores Hidalgo here in 1810, and San Miguel de Allende nearby is a UNESCO site.
From Nahuatl xalixco, "on the sandy surface" — xalli is sand.
Tequila comes from the town of Tequila here, and by law from this state and small parts of four others, from blue agave only.
Mariachi, the charreada rodeo and the wide sombrero are all Jalisco's, which is why they read worldwide as simply Mexican.
Probably Purépecha k'erhi-iretarhu, "place of the great town", though a Nahuatl derivation about a ball game is also offered.
Its aqueduct of 74 arches, built in the 1720s, still frames the city, and the historic centre is a UNESCO site.
Mexico's 1917 constitution was written here, and Maximilian was executed on a hill just outside in 1867.

A Spanish mishearing: asked the land's name, the Maya are said to have answered something like "I don't understand you" — the story is probably too neat, but the name is certainly not Maya for anything.
Chichén Itzá is here, and its pyramid throws a serpent-shaped shadow down its stairs at the equinoxes.
The asteroid that ended the dinosaurs struck off its north coast; the crater's rim is still traceable as a ring of cenotes.
For Miguel Hidalgo, the priest who called for independence in 1810.
Real del Monte here was worked by Cornish miners from 1824, who left behind pasties — now sold as pastes — and Mexico's first football pitch.
The Tula site in it has 4.6 m stone warriors on top of its pyramid, from the Toltec capital.
"True cross" — Cortés landed on Good Friday 1519 and named the first Spanish town in the mainland Americas for it.
Everything Spain took out of Mexico left through this port for three hundred years, and everything African and Caribbean came in: son jarocho music is the result.
Pico de Orizaba on its border is Mexico's highest mountain at 5,636 m, and vanilla was first cultivated by the Totonac here.
For Andrés Quintana Roo, a poet and independence-era politician — the only state named for a writer.
Cancún was an uninhabited sandbar until 1970, when a computer model picked it as the best site for a resort.
The Mesoamerican Reef offshore is the second-longest barrier reef in the world, and Sian Ka'an behind it is a UNESCO biosphere.
From Nahuatl texcalli, "place of maize tortillas" or of crags, depending on which reading you take.
The smallest state, and the one that allied with Cortés against the Aztecs — which is why its people were never conquered and got privileges the rest did not.
Cacaxtla in it holds battle murals in Maya style, painted around 650, among the best-preserved in Mesoamerica.
Short for Puebla de los Ángeles, "town of the angels" — founded in 1531 as a Spanish town with no indigenous settlement underneath it.
Cinco de Mayo commemorates the 1862 battle here, where a smaller Mexican force beat the French army.
Cholula beside it has the largest pyramid by volume in the world, with a church built on top of it — the Spanish thought it was a hill.
The state that surrounds the capital and shares the country's name, from Mexica, the Aztecs' own name for themselves.
Teotihuacán is here — a city of over 100,000 people by 400 AD, already abandoned and legendary when the Aztecs found it and gave it its name.
The most populous state in the country, and it wraps around Mexico City on three sides.
The federal district — now officially just Ciudad de México, renamed in 2016, but the map keeps the older label.
It is built on the drained lake bed of Tenochtitlán and is sinking up to 50 cm a year in places; the cathedral leans visibly.
Its Zócalo is one of the largest city squares in the world, and Chapultepec is one of the largest urban parks.
From Maya kaan peech, "place of snakes and ticks", which its founders presumably hoped visitors would not look up.
Its walled city was fortified in the 1600s against pirates and is a UNESCO site, still ringed by bastions.
Calakmul in its jungle was one of the two Maya superpowers, rival of Tikal, and its main pyramid rises above the canopy.
From Nahuatl michhuahcān, "place of the fishermen" — the Purépecha lived around its lakes.
The Purépecha were never conquered by the Aztecs, and their language is unrelated to any other.
Monarch butterflies from Canada and the United States winter in its fir forests, tens of millions of them on a few hectares.
Probably from Nahuatl coliman, "place conquered by our grandfathers", or from a local ruler's name.
The second smallest state, and its Volcán de Colima is one of the most active in North America.
It administers the Revillagigedo islands, a UNESCO site 700 km offshore that is Mexico's largest marine reserve.
For José María Morelos, the priest who took over the independence war after Hidalgo was shot.
Cuernavaca's mild weather made it the retreat of Aztec emperors, then Cortés, then Maximilian — it is called the city of eternal spring.
Emiliano Zapata was born here, and his land-reform slogan tierra y libertad came out of this state's sugar estates.
Probably from a chief called Tabscoob, or a Nahuatl phrase for damp earth — the sauce is named after the state.
The Olmecs, the first Mesoamerican civilisation, were here 3,000 years ago and carved the colossal basalt heads.
It is the wettest state: about a third of all the water in Mexico's rivers flows through it.
For Vicente Guerrero, an independence leader of African and indigenous descent who became president and abolished slavery in 1829.
Acapulco was the Pacific end of the Manila galleon route for 250 years, bringing Asian silk and porcelain to Spain across two oceans.
Its Taxco is a silver town of white houses on a steep hill, and the state has some of the deepest poverty in Mexico.
From Nahuatl huaxyacac, "at the nose of the guaje tree", a pod-bearing tree still common there.
The most linguistically diverse state in Mexico: sixteen indigenous language groups, and many of its towns govern by customary law rather than party politics.
Monte Albán above the city was the Zapotec capital, and the state is the home of mole, mezcal and Día de Muertos as the world pictures it.
From Nahuatl chiapan, "on the chia water" — chia being the seed, which grew along its river.
Palenque here has the tomb of Pakal, whose carved sarcophagus lid is among the most famous objects in the Maya world.
The Zapatista uprising began here on 1 January 1994, and the state grows most of Mexico's coffee.
